stories.title_en: Posing as Daoists to Swindle the Salt Inspector

paragraphs.en: Tang Yin, courtesy name Bohu, also Ziwei, was from Wuqu Lane in Nanjing. He topped the Nanjing provincial examination in the wuwu year of the Hongzhi reign (1498) but lost his degree due to a scandal. Thereafter he lived unbridled, drifting through life in revelry and wine. Skilled in poetry and prose, his painting was especially fine. He befriended Wen Zhengming, Wen Zhengzhong, Zhu Xizhe, and others—all the most famous figures of their day. He spent his days visiting pleasure houses, amusing himself with jokes and composing off the cuff. A yamen runner once brought a sheet of paper asking for a painting. Bohu took up the brush, painted a dozen or so snails, and wrote on it: "Not a swimming crab, not a razor clam; among seafood this one barely has a name. Call a thousand times, ten thousand times, it will not come out; it only waits for someone to smack its rump." Everyone laughed hard. One day he went out and saw a monk in a cangue in front of the county yamen. People asked him to compose a poem about the monk. Bohu learned why the monk had been cangued, then wrote on the cangue: "A runner, sent on official business, went to pick tea; he wanted no fine silver, only credit. The county seized him for thirty strokes; on a square tray they served up a big watermelon." The magistrate, seeing guests out, noticed it, asked who had written it, was told it was Bohu, and promptly released the monk. His ready tongue was generally of this kind.

One day, with Zhu Xizhe and a dozen others, he packed up and traveled to Yangzhou. Day after day they drank with courtesans and took their pleasure in music and beauty. After nearly a month their funds were almost exhausted. Xizhe said, "The gold is spent—what's the plan?" Bohu said, "No matter. The salt inspector these days has tens of thousands in wealth. You and I can pretend to be Daoist priests from Nüzhen Abbey to swindle him." The two dressed as Daoists. When the salt inspector held court, they prostrated themselves at the foot of the steps and announced, "Daoist priests of Nüzhen Abbey present themselves." The salt inspector was furious: "Have you not heard that a censor's court is severe as frost? What kind of Daoists dare such insolence!" He was about to have them beaten. The two answered calmly: "Does Your Honor take us for wandering beggar-priests seeking alms? We have traveled the whole empire; those we keep company with are all the most famous men in the land. Even Tang Bohu, Wen Zhengming, and Zhu Xizhe of Wu county set aside their rank to befriend us. Poetry, lyrics, songs, rhapsodies—we finish them the moment we open our mouths. If Your Honor does not believe us, we offer a modest sample; command us as you please." The salt inspector pointed to a stone ox below the hall as the topic and ordered them to compose a linked verse. Bohu answered at once: "A towering strange rock leans against the clouds." Zhe: "Thrown down—who can tell how many years by now." Hu: "Moss on the terrace makes its hair, grown by the rain." Zhe: "Vines thread its nose, left for the wind to tug." Hu: "It has never eaten grass beside the stream." Zhe: "From of old it could never plow the ridge fields." Hu: "No wonder the herdboy's whip cannot raise it." Zhe: "The sound of his flute hangs aslant in the sunset haze."

The salt inspector finished reading, his expression cleared, and he asked, "The poem is fine. What do you want?" The two said, "Nüzhen Abbey has lately fallen into ruin. We hear Your Honor is generous and fond of giving. If you would give from your salary to repair it, it would complete a worthy deed, and the merit would not fade." The salt inspector was delighted and issued a dispatch to the two counties of Wuxing: they were to issue five hundred taels from the treasury to them. Seeing that he had agreed, the two hurried that very night to Wuxing, using their guise as Daoists to cite their official backing and told the two counties: "The salt inspector is repairing Nüzhen Abbey. This is a grand undertaking. Give the sum as ordered; do not delay." The two counties paid it in full. The two men, delighted with the silver, said, "If we had not risked the ten-thousand-fathom pool, how would we have got the pearl under the black dragon's chin?" They went back to Yangzhou, gathered their dozen companions, shouted and drank in the courtesans' houses, indulging in unrestrained pleasure. In fewer than ten days the five hundred taels were gone. Later the salt inspector came through Wuxing on tour, put on his robes and cap, and went to Nüzhen Abbey—only to find it still in ruins as before. He summoned the two magistrates and rebuked them. They answered, "The other day Tang Bohu and Zhu Xizhe came from Yangzhou and praised Your Honor for raising this grand work; we magistrates paid the sum as ordered." The salt inspector was dismayed. He knew he had been taken in by the two men, but he valued their talent, so he did not pursue it.

Note: Tang Bohu and Zhu Xizhe were both famous masters of their generation throughout the land. Blocked in their careers, they gave themselves over to music and beauty; there was no brothel or tavern that had not heard their names. Yet without tongues eloquent as a flowing river, and talent ready to compose at a moment’s notice, how could they have shaken the inspector’s yamen? This swindle may be called a swindle well done. Think of the men who wear official caps and sit on tiger skins today: they all think of scraping the people’s fat to grease their private purses, gathering the crowd’s resentment to fatten their own households—and how they cheat the people! Then one day they themselves are taken in by Tang and Zhu, which may serve as a warning to the greedy. That the inspector knew and still did not pursue it may also be called a heart that pities talent.

stories.title_en: Chen Quan Leaves a Parting Trick After Visiting a Famous Courtesan

paragraphs.en: Chen Quan of Jinling was a man of enormous wealth. He was dashing and easy in his ways, and especially good at jokes. Whatever he saw, he could turn into an improvised verse at once. He used to keep company with the local courtesans; one of them was his particular favorite. In summer, when the first melons came in, the brothel placed two pieces of melon rind just inside the threshold and had someone run to Quan in a panic: "A certain sister has suddenly taken a mortal illness; she wants to see you once before she can close her eyes." Quan mounted at once and rode hard. He rushed in, stepped on the rind, and fell. The courtesans clapped and laughed: "Master Chen, make a verse at once—no delay!" Quan answered: "Chen Quan came in a rush; the brothel had it all arranged. Just because of two pieces of rind, I nearly lost my life." The women were delighted; they drank together and left it at that.

Another day he was out on the lake with several courtesans and saw a newly built boat. They said, "Make a verse at once—don't lag!" Quan answered: "A brand-new little boat; at first it was meant to pick red lotuses. Now it is a ferry at the crossing, coming and going endlessly. Those with money it takes aboard; those without it tosses aside. Wet above, leaking below, never dry—and from the far bank another gentleman is calling." The courtesans all laughed and admired him. His joking verses were generally of this kind.

At that time, Hangzhou in Zhejiang had a famous courtesan named Hua Buru. She was a great beauty and versed in the qin, chess, poetry, and painting. Her price was high; she did not associate with ordinary men, only with the wealthy and distinguished. A night with her cost six or seven taels. Quan heard of her and wanted to sleep with her, so he set out to cheat her. He arranged for more than a dozen household servants to send boats to Hangzhou one after another, while he and two or three servants went first. At Hua Buru's house, he ordered a leather chest carried into her bedroom—the bottom layers were paper packets filled with bricks and stones, while the top layer contained paper packets of real silver, ten taels per packet. In front of everyone, he opened the chest, took out silver, tipped the household servants very generously, and presented Buru with ten taels of silver. Buru and the servants were all delighted, thinking this was a great rich man and that what they would get would be beyond counting. Buru asked, "Where is the gentleman from?" Quan said, "Jinling." "Your surname?" "Lang." "Your style name?" "Zisui." Buru laid out a rich feast. Zisui did not leave; he stayed at her house. After two days, another servant came to report: "Boat number such-and-such has arrived." Zisui said, "Leave the rest of the goods on the boat; just carry the leather chests into Sister's house." This happened three or four times until five or six chests were in Buru's bedroom. Zisui saw Buru wearing pearls and said, "These pearls of yours are all poor stuff. I have several hundred large pearls, every one of them round. When this next boat arrives, I will fetch them for you."

After more than a month, Zisui had his fill. A servant came to report: "Boat number such-and-such has arrived." Zisui said to Buru, "This boat is not like the earlier ones; it carries only genuine treasure. I must go look myself and fetch the large pearls for you. The several leather chests are in your bedroom; you must watch them. I won't be back until afternoon. Just send one of your men and a mount with me." Buru sent a man and a donkey to accompany Zisui.

Halfway there, Zisui hurriedly said, "I left a key in your mistress's room. I set out in a rush and forgot to bring it; you must go back and fetch it." The servant turned to go. Zisui called out, "Wait! You will need a note in my own hand, or your mistress will not hand the key over to you. Otherwise, you will never get it." Zisui dismounted from the donkey, went into a paper shop, and wrote a verse: "Hangzhou's Hua Buru took in Jintai's prodigal Zisui; she fell for the man and lost a donkey too. From this parting on, where will she find her bright pearls?" He sealed it and sent the man back. Buru opened it, realized she had been swindled, and hurriedly opened the leather chests—inside were nothing but bricks and stones. Zisui had already ordered his men to hire a boat and wait; as soon as he reached the river, he boarded and headed back to the capital. Later, Buru inquired carefully and learned it was Chen Quan of Nanjing, but there was nothing she could do.

Note: Brothels routinely cheat others—in minor cases ruining a family, in major ones costing a life—yet one never hears of them being cheated themselves. Hua Buru, moreover, set her price high and handpicked her patrons; the wealth she extracted from men was beyond counting. Who would have thought Chen Quan possessed tricks even more uncanny, appearing and vanishing like a spirit? She lost both her lover and her donkey, and regret came too late. Though this was a piece of unruly mischief on Chen Quan's part, it still provides a good laugh at the expense of the pleasure houses that ensnare others.
